title: Heartbeat stall, pipelining & egress shaping tail latency hunt - Borealis Telecom
summary: Deep-dive to root-cause intermittent p99 spikes observed in Borealis' VPC-hosted Redwood inference endpoints. Focused on heartbeat-driven stalls during pipelined streaming, network policing (egress shaping) interactions, and KV cache hotkey behavior. Agreed next steps: run controlled replay with packet captures + KV diagnostics, test streaming off vs batching high-concurrency, and share benchmark template + security docs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-14 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Dylan (PM), Zoe (Redwood SRE enablement), Samir (CTO), Laura (Platform), Miguel (SRE), Priya (ML Infra), Ethan (Network)
---
Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): intermittent p99 spikes on streaming endpoints, appears correlated with short bursts of network egress shaping and KV cache thrash. Possible handshake/pipelining stall when stream open/close coincides with egress throttle.
---
Topics: p95/p99 tail, streaming vs non-streaming, KV hotkeys/eviction, pipelining stalls, egress shaping, quantization tradeoffs, VPC topology
---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving time. we'll call this the heartbeat stall and pipelining tail hunt. quick roll call?
[00:12] Samir (Borealis): Samir here. we jump right in, we've been seeing elastic p99 jumps after about 30k requests, mostly in the 10- to 50-millisecond extra tail range but sporadic to 200ms.
[00:30] Ravi (Redwood): ok that's the number—are these on streaming endpoints, non-streaming, or both?
[00:35] Laura (Borealis): primarily streaming; non-streaming is kinda stable. we do sometimes fallback to non-streaming during incidents but still see small bumps.
[00:45] Zoe (Redwood): and the endpoints are in your VPC private deployment, right? can you confirm if it's the private (customer VPC) plane or dedicated redwood-managed?
[00:55] Miguel (Borealis): It's our VPC private deployment, we manage egress via a network appliance that does policing/shape. we suspect that maybe the egress shaping interacts poorly with the persistent streaming handshakes.
[01:08] Ravi: ok good clue. can you describe the streaming implementation? are you using chunked transfer with an open HTTP/2 stream or SSE?
[01:18] Priya (Borealis): we use HTTP/2 streaming with chunked frames, we then proxy through our sidecar that does TLS termination->mTLS to upstream.
[01:28] Ethan (Network): and that sidecar occasionally gets burst-policed — we have an egress profile that throttles short high-burst flows to protect peering links.
[01:36] Maya: perfect — so picture: long-lived streaming connections, intermittent egress shaping that can add micro-pauses. concurrent pipelining in the inference runtime expects continuous token flow; a micro-pause can trigger a slow path like re-sync/heartbeat, does that fit what you see?
[01:52] Samir: yes, sometimes we see stalls that look like 100-300ms where the request is otherwise sitting idle. we thought it was KV cache spike but network looks correlated in our dashboards.
[02:05] Ravi: let's walk through hypothesis matrix. possible causes: 1) KV cache hotkey eviction leading to cold KV reads on hot shard; 2) streaming handshake/ping timeouts or retries when a packet is dropped; 3) sidecar egress shaping causing head-of-line backpressure; 4) quantization-induced compute jitter (less likely but worth checking).
[02:22] Laura: yeah, we have a few heavy prefixes that create hot keys in KV — some sessions access same prefix. eviction policy is LRU with 2GB shard.
[02:30] Zoe: do you have KV metrics by key or only per-shard aggregates?
[02:34] Miguel: only aggregates right now, we can enable key-level counters but worry about cost.
[02:40] Ravi: ok enabling key counters for a short window is worth it. we want to see whether the p99 aligns to a hotkey eviction — warm cache will have sub-ms KV hits, cold read can add 10-20ms depending on storage. but you said the jumps are up to 200ms, which suggests something else layered on top.
[02:59] Maya: what about the streaming protocol timeouts/heartbeat intervals? if the runtime expects regular tiny keep-alives and the sidecar buffers/polices, the runtime could stall waiting for next chunk and trigger internal requeue.
[03:12] Priya: our heartbeat is default 60s at app level but the runtime does a millisecond-level pipelining window. can you elaborate on pipelining?
[03:20] Ravi: sure — Redwood runtime opens several async windows where token generation, KV lookups, and GPU kernel launches are overlapped. If a token frame is delayed, the pipeline can block waiting for the KV response or the next model chunk. That stall then propagates to subsequent requests in the same worker until the pipeline flushes. In streaming mode, that flush is seen as an extra tail.
[03:40] Ethan: so a 30-100ms buffer in network could ripple as p99. makes sense.
[03:46] Samir: is there a recommended buffer/read-ahead we should tune on sidecar or runtime to avoid these ripples?
[03:52] Ravi: there are knobs on both sides. On runtime: reduce kernel prefetching windows, increase KV read-ahead, or enable partial-response streaming that can emit tokens before full KV resolution for non-critical keys. On network: avoid aggressive burst policing for long-lived streams; add token-bucket sizing for those flows.
[04:10] Maya: practical first step — can we run an A/B: streamed traffic untouched vs streamed with buffering at sidecar (small epoll window) vs non-streaming batched calls? We'll correlate p95/p99 and KV hit rates.
[04:22] Miguel: yes we can. we have a staging cluster mirroring prod.
[04:26] Laura: question — what about quantization? we've heard quantized kernels sometimes have more variability in per-token times especially at short sequences.
[04:34] Ravi: quantization adds some variance because some activation paths pick slower kernels, and the runtime's kernel selector may choose alternative fused ops. on average it's faster and cheaper, but tail can be slightly larger if you have heterogenous seq lengths. usually that contributes single-digit ms variance, not 200ms.
[04:51] Priya: ok good, we were worried.
[04:55] Dylan (Redwood PM): can we talk about the interaction between KV hotkeys and pipelining? When a hotkey misses, does the runtime stall entire pipeline or single request?
[05:04] Ravi: depends on how KV is accessed. If KV is synchronous in the critical path, it can stall the worker thread. We have async KV primitives that allow speculative continuation for some paths. But if application logic blocks until KV returns (e.g., user-level prefix lookups used to select prompt templates), that blocks. Speculative tokens may help but change semantics.
[05:23] Maya: any evidence you can share that indicates blocking KV calls?
[05:27] Miguel: our app does a prompt template lookup per session start; generally it's cached but some sessions miss and go to DB. Not huge but bursts coincide with p99.
[05:36] Ravi: cool, that's actionable. Enable per-key counters and short TTL on template keys to reduce eviction cascades. Also consider moving hot prefixes into a dedicated shard to limit eviction impact.
[05:48] Samir: about shard sizing — is it possible to pin a shard to a worker to reduce cross-shard latency?
[05:55] Zoe: yes you can create shard affinity. downside is load imbalance if a hot shard gets all requests. but for templates it's fine.
[06:03] Ethan: network question — we've seen our peering provider apply microburst mitigation at the egress edge sometimes after sustained rate. it kills short high-rate flows. would that behave differently for HTTP/1 chunked vs HTTP/2 frames?
[06:15] Ravi: HTTP/2 multiplexing might exacerbate head-of-line because many concurrent logical streams share connection, so a policing pause on connection level stops multiple streams at once. HTTP/1 persistent with multiple connections may spread risk but have other overheads.
[06:30] Laura: hmm interesting — we used HTTP/2 to keep conn count low. maybe we need to try multi-connection approach.
[06:35] Maya: note — Redwood runtime supports multiplexing but we can fall back to per-request connections as experiment. small tradeoff in open file descriptors.
[06:43] Miguel: I'd prefer to test in staging.
[06:47] [sound of short crosstalk]
[06:52] Ravi: ok next let's walk through a minimal diagnostic plan that we can execute quickly: 1) enable per-key KV counters for 12h window; 2) run streaming traffic replay with and without sidecar policing; 3) capture tcpdump on sidecar for p99 windows; 4) collect runtime traces from Redwood agent (pipeline latencies, kernel selection logs).
[07:12] Samir: timeline?
[07:14] Maya: we'll share the benchmark template today, you run the replay, capture pcaps, and share, and we analyze. plan for initial analysis in 5 business days.
[07:22] Priya: on the runtime traces — what format? flamegraphs?
[07:25] Ravi: yes, we'll ask you to install our lightweight agent that emits per-request histograms and a small trace file (flamegraph friendly). it doesn't send payloads, just timings and key ids hashed.
[07:37] Miguel: ok security is a must — will this agent send any PII?
[07:41] Zoe: agent is telemetry-only; payloads are hashed or omitted. we'll provide the security whitepaper.
[07:48] Samir: any hard SLOs we should plan for once this is mitigated? we'd like p99 under 50ms with 95th under 20ms for streaming. realistic?
[07:58] Ravi: yes likely achievable with two mitigations: reduce egress shaping impact and isolate hot KV keys. also tune runtime pipeline windows. For heavy loads you may still see rare spikes because of network microbursts, but we can get tail into 30–50ms.
[08:12] Maya: question from Dylan — would a batching non-streamed path yield better tail behavior for you?
[08:17] Dylan: yes in general non-streaming batched calls move variance into queueing, which can reduce p99 for user-perceived latency but increase median. depends on UX tolerance.
[08:27] Laura: for our real-time chat product, median matters as much as tail; users notice pauses. so can't move to high-latency batching.
[08:35] Ravi: consider hybrid — small batch windows (e.g., 16–32ms) to absorb microbursts, plus streaming fast-path for low-latency tokens. Redwood has a microbatching mode that may help.
[08:47] Priya: sounds promising. how does microbatching interact with KV?
[08:51] Ravi: it reduces per-request context switches and allows the runtime to amortize KV lookups across microbatches — but semantics must allow coalescing. not always feasible for session-specific templates.
[09:03] Maya: let's pause and go into a concrete example — Miguel, can you share a recent p99 event timeline from your monitoring?
[09:10] Miguel: yes pulling up. timeline: 14:02:34 - small spike in outbound bytes, 14:02:34.120 - p99 jump recorded, 14:02:34.140 - sidecar reported 200ms egress pause, 14:02:34.320 - runtime pipeline flush event.
[09:30] Ravi: that aligns—sidecar pause then pipeline flush. do you also have KV eviction events at that time?
[09:36] Miguel: not in aggregate, but we don't have key-level counters enabled then.
[09:40] Ravi: ok that points to primary hypothesis: network egress shaping causes streaming micro-pauses that lead to pipeline stalls, which magnify tail. Secondary hypothesis: occasional hotkey eviction amplifies duration.
[09:52] Maya: what defensive config can you toggle quickly?
[09:55] Ravi: 1) change sidecar to apply token-bucket at connection granularity and exempt long-lived streams; 2) enable connection-level buffering to smooth microbursts; 3) on runtime set pipeline max-blocking-ms to a lower threshold so delayed tokens fail-fast and fall back to non-streaming path (safer UX tradeoff).
[10:14] Ethan: exempting long-lived streams is doable on our edge policy.
[10:17] Laura: buffer introduces latency — how big? 10ms?
[10:20] Ravi: small ring buffer of 8-16KB adds ~1-4ms at typical rates, but smooths microbursts. choose size with caution.
[10:29] Dylan: important to measure user-level effect. Maya — we'll provide the benchmark template with 3 scenarios: baseline streaming, streaming+buffer, and non-streaming microbatching.
[10:39] Maya: ok adding that to next steps.
[10:42] [short pause]
[10:45] Priya: one more question — about quantization: if we fall back to a quantized variant for cost reasons, should we expect different tail characteristics?
[10:52] Ravi: quantized kernels sometimes pick different FMA/loop unrolls; on GPU this can mean slightly different jitter due to occupancy. again usually single-digit ms differences. If your p99 contributor is network/pipeline, quantization won't fix it. but quantization reduces average GPU time which may reduce contention in heavy throughput scenarios.
[11:10] Miguel: good to know.
[11:12] Maya: we'll also share a quick checklist for KV: per-key metrics enabled for short window, consider pinning known hot keys, add small TTL to templates, and shard affinity for hot prefixes.
[11:25] Laura: can Redwood agent suggest shard assignment recommendations?
[11:28] Ravi: yes, we can run a hot-key analysis script — it reports skew and suggests shard splits or pinning. we'll include that in the package.
[11:38] Samir: do you have known cases where egress shaping caused similar issues for other customers?
[11:42] Maya: yes, we saw a telco customer last quarter where peering microbursts plus HTTP/2 multiplexing produced p99 spikes; they reduced mitigation by splitting streams across multiple connections and tuning sidecar token buckets. we'll anonymize that case study and share.
[11:56] Dylan: note for product — maybe runtime should detect prolonged micro-pauses and auto-fallback to non-streaming until pipe recovers. Ravi, is that on the roadmap?
